subject: 03AC86CF18154B14AB43126BC79D41F8
introduction: “We follow Christ and not the priests.” These eighteen passages measure Christian ministry by Christ’s own life: he was hungry and homeless and crowned with thorns, and those who speak in his name ride in gilded carriages and wear jewels; he said to love enemies, and popes made war. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that many popes were holy, and invites one minister to become “a heavenly clergyman”. Nothing in the critique is new to Christians: its texts are the Gospel’s own woes against chief seats and whited sepulchres, Ezekiel’s shepherds who feed themselves, Milton’s hungry sheep, Dostoevsky’s Inquisitor. Chaucer’s parson and the standard in the letter to Timothy are here because the tradition also knows what a good minister is. And Paul’s account of the Lord’s Supper is set beside reading 8 so that the rite it criticizes is heard in Christian words.
questions: Every charge in these readings can be found in the Gospels and in Christian writers. What difference does it make whether such criticism comes from inside a community or from outside?
Reading 15 says, “There were many holy men among the Popes, but not all.” How does that sentence change the way the rest should be read?
Reading 8 describes the Eucharist as an outsider sees it. Put Paul’s words beside it. What would a fair description by a non-Christian need to include?
Chaucer’s parson “first … wroghte, and afterward he taughte”. What does reading 2 ask of the minister it addresses?

outside.why: “We follow Christ and not the priests.” Peter and the apostles before the high priest: we ought to obey God rather than men.
A minister is invited to become “a heavenly clergyman”. English literature’s best-loved portrait of one is Chaucer’s poor parson, who taught Christ’s lore, but first he followed it himself.
“Ordained Ministers are many, confirmed Ministers are few.” Many are called, but few are chosen.
Christ lived on the herbs of the wilderness; the Pope rides in a gilded carriage. Peter at the temple gate: silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee.
The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.

Christ’s crown was of thorns and his garment torn; the cardinal’s is jewelled. They stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe; and when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head.
Jesus on religious dress and rank in his own day: they make broad their phylacteries, and love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats.

Many clergy, it is said, cannot breathe one breath of the disciples. The Church’s own standard is not lower than the reading’s: a bishop must be blameless, vigilant, sober, given to hospitality, not greedy of filthy lucre. By whose measure are the clergy being found wanting, an outsider’s or their own?

The priests’ words over bread and wine are named as a cause of irreligion. To Christians this is obedience: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. The reading reports the rite as an outsider sees it. How would a communicant describe what is done?
They “know only the letter”. The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
Missionary colleges teach students that their parents’ religions are false. Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte.
They look on Easterners as heathen. Peter, who had thought the same of Romans: of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.
The clergy tied their fortunes to the state and fell with it. Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!
The divines of the age “have become corrupt and have corrupted others”. They be blind leaders of the blind; and if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
Christ commanded the other cheek; popes shed blood. Put up again thy sword into his place. The reading adds, fairly, that many popes were holy men.
Christ opened heaven; the cardinal opens a church, to applause. Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor to the returned Christ: why hast Thou come to hinder us?
Congregations are compared to the Pharisees. Jesus’s charge against them was of an outside unlike the inside: whited sepulchres, beautiful outward.
Leaders who once enlightened others are dissolved when a new sun rises. Milton on a clergy that had stopped feeding: the hungry sheep look up, and are not fed.
